lines.text: Twenty-seven floors up, across the road from a Hong Kong racetrack, two men are watching a computer, not the race.
Bill Benter started out counting cards in Las Vegas, until the casinos blacklisted him.
So he went looking for a game where the house couldn't throw him out: horse racing in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong bet more on horses than the entire United States.
And it's a pool.
Bettors play against each other, while the club keeps about seventeen percent.
To win, Benter had to beat the crowd by more than that.
He taught himself statistics.
Two typists spent nine months entering thousands of old races.
In nineteen eighty-five, he flew in with three computers in his luggage.
The first season, he and his partner lost a hundred and twenty thousand dollars.
The answer was hiding in plain sight: the crowd's own odds.
His model stopped ignoring the public and started correcting it.
One season, he says, that was worth about three million dollars.
The club didn't ban him.
It called him one of its best customers, and let him plug his computers straight into its betting system.
His model grew to more than a hundred and twenty factors per horse.
In nineteen ninety-seven, the club suspended his account.
So his team printed betting slips and fed them into machines by hand, minutes before each race.
Which brings us back to that night in two thousand one.
Their computer had placed fifty-one thousand bets on one giant jackpot.
One of them hit: sixteen million dollars.
Benter never cashed it.
"It would be unsporting," he said.
The tickets went into a safe, and the money went to charity.
His operations made close to a billion dollars.
So the next time you bet on a horse, who else is in that pool with you?
